rv.q: It’s a hugely enjoyable – and yes, scary – piece of theatre horror entertainment...
It Walks Around the House At Night is a deliciously spine-tingling triumph of stagecraft.
The result is an engrossing, intriguing and highly entertaining show that steadily builds suspense and uses its narrator to balance plausibility and incredulity.

There’s some great stage trickery deployed on the set designed by Tom Robbins and director Neil Bettles, which ensures that the impacts of lighting and video projection by Joshua Pharo are fully maximised.
An impressive and energetic production that doesn't rely on suddenly cranking up the volume to make patrons jump – it's far more slick and sophisticated than that.
It Walks Around the House at Night provides plenty of atmospheric tension and more than its fair share of jump scares.
The humour undermines the horror, and a slew of anecdotes about his work and love life mean the whole thing lacks immediacy.
It’s unclear why this pamphleteering drivel is being presented as a ghost story.

cn.t: Critics hail this spine-tingling horror as a stagecraft triumph that capitalizes on theatre's current appetite for scares, though some find it over-explains its mysteries and shows the ghost too readily when subtlety might have worked better.
